title: Miharban's telling
hookLine: a janamsakhi from the line of Prithi Chand, more reflective, full of discourse

lines: THE UNCLE WHO FELL OUT WITH EVERYONE.
A TELLING FROM A RIVAL LINE.
cards: Families have them: the uncle who fell out with everyone over the will, years ago. Nobody quite forgives him.

And yet, when the old photos come out, he's the one who remembers the names, the places, what grandfather used to say at the table. You'd rather not need him. But he kept the old papers, and he's thought hard about them.
Sikh history has a telling of Guru Nanak's life that comes from a line like that. Today: Miharban's telling.

teach.h: PRITHI CHAND, GURU ARJAN'S ELDER BROTHER.
teach.b: Start with the family. Prithi Chand was the elder brother of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru. When Guru Ram Das chose Arjan as the next Guru, Prithi Chand did not accept it, and his line set itself up apart.
Sikh tradition remembers them as rivals to the Gurus.

teach.h: MIHARBAN, HIS SON, AND HIS TELLING.
teach.b: Miharban was Prithi Chand's son, and a janamsakhi comes down under his name. It doesn't read like the plain Puratan stories or the warm, wonder-filled Bala ones. It's reflective.
A sakhi sets the scene, and then the telling stops to talk: a discourse, a gosht, in which Guru Nanak's own hymns are explained in the setting of the story.
It reads less like a storyteller and more like a teacher thinking aloud.
So how do Sikhs read a book from that line? Carefully, and not all in the same way. Some keep their distance from it because of where it came from.

Some historians and readers take it seriously as one more early witness, and value its long reflections on Nanak's hymns. Neither group pretends the family quarrel didn't happen. Here's the lesson in it.
A telling from someone you'd rather not agree with can still add something: a detail, a reading, a question. Taking it in isn't the same as taking their side.
And every telling adds something of its teller too, which is exactly why it's worth knowing who the teller was.

how: Scholars of Sikh history read Miharban's janamsakhi alongside the other traditions, mindful of its origin in the line of Prithi Chand, and some draw on its discourses on Guru Nanak's hymns.

o: a telling in a companion's own voice
a reflective janamsakhi from a rival line
the oldest and plainest life of Nanak

games.q: the family and the book — tap the pairs.

games.q: a rival branch of your family writes a thoughtful book about the teacher your family follows. what do you do with it?
o: read it carefully, knowing who wrote it.
believe every word because it's thoughtful.
games.why: Sikhs and historians who use Miharban's telling read it carefully, mindful of its origin: taking it in isn't taking sides.

practice: Bring one person to mind, not someone dangerous, just someone whose views or choices you'd rather not share: a relative, a coworker, a voice you usually scroll past.
Ask yourself one honest question, what might they know or notice that I don't, and let one possibility come; you don't have to agree with it, only hear it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.
